Asian-ish Identity of Myers + Chang Myers + Chang
1145 Washington St, Boston

Myers + Chang’s Construction of Asian-ish Identity through Language, Literacy, and Writings

❖
MYERS + CHANG Exterior Window Sign picture from: https://www.myersandchang.com/about/
Myers + Chang Dining Room & Window Dragon Design Field Observation Photograph
Central Claim

Myers + Chang constructs its unique “Asian-ish” identity through intentional multimodal linguistic and literacy practices that combine traditional Asian heritage with entertaining, Westernized culinary and literary conventions in the restaurant's name, menu design, dish naming, decorations, dining atmosphere, as well as spoken interactions within the restaurant and written communication across various platforms.

Context

Myers + Chang is a Chinese restaurant located at 1145 Washington St, Boston. Opened in 2007, it is the collaborative venture of the renowned pastry chef and James Beard Award winner Joanne Chang and her spouse, longtime Boston restaurant owner Christopher Myers, her husband, a longtime Boston restaurant owner. Instead of serving strictly traditional Asian cuisine, it positions itself as "Asian-ish" and serves plates that blend Chinese, Taiwanese, Thai, and Vietnamese influences.

Joanne Chang

An honors graduate of Harvard College with a degree in Applied Mathematics and Economics, Joanne left a career as a management consultant to enter the world of professional cooking as a garde-manger cook at Boston’s renowned Biba restaurant. In addition to Myers + Chang, she operated 9 Flour bakeries in Boston/Cambridge in Boston’s South End.

picture from: https://www.myersandchang.com/about/

Christopher Myers

Christopher has been in and out of the hospitality business for 40 years. Prior to opening Myers+Chang in 2007, he created and co-owned 4 iconic and award-winning Boston-area restaurants: Rialto, Radius, Via Matta, and Great Bay. Christopher began a partnership with Joanne Chang in 2006, in which they created a second Flour Bakery.

During my visit to Myers + Chang, I tasted its popular dishes, talked to customers enjoying their dinner, and interviewed several waiters and waitresses from different national backgrounds. Based on my notes and interviews, I find one interesting thing about Myers + Chang: It defines itself as "Asian-ish." Myers + Chang constructs its unique “Asian-ish” identity through intentional linguistic and literacy practices that intertwine culinary terms, cultural allusions, artistic elements, and oral communication in the restaurant with written communication across platforms. Deliberate linguistic practices include the restaurant’s name as a bilingual and bicultural marker and its self-positioning as "Asian-ish.” Culinary terminology involves the use of specialized vocabulary on the menu. Cultural references deal with references to traditions of different Asian nations on the menu and Asian arts in the restaurant decoration. Written communication across platforms discusses the restaurant and reinforces its Asian-ish identity through social media and press materials.

Deliberate Linguistic Choices of Myers + Chang

Christopher Myers & Joanne Chang picture from: https://www.myersandchang.com/about/
Exterior “MYERS + CHANG” Window Sign picture from: https://www.myersandchang.com/about/

Myers + Chang creates its unique “Asian-ish” identity through deliberate linguistic choices. As soon as I approached the restaurant, I saw that the restaurant's exterior had a large “MYERS + CHANG” sign visible through the front window. In my interview with Kevin, the manager of Myers + Chang, he told me that the restaurant’s name “Myers + Chang” celebrated its “Asian-ish" identity, which was shaped by the founders' diverse, cross-cultural experiences.

Myers is the surname of Chang’s husband, Christopher Myers, an Anglo-American. Chang is the surname of Joanne Chang, a Taiwanese American. The deliberate pairing of an Anglo surname and a Chinese surname is a clear representation of the founders’ desire to integrate their unique cultures and embrace a diverse culinary and personal identity. "Myers" is a symbol of the American business partner and co-owner, Christopher Myers, whereas "Chang" is an allusion to the Taiwanese ancestry of the chef Joanne Chang. Such a dual naming creates, at the very beginning, the impression that the establishment navigates between the cultural traditions instead of following one fixed linguistic or culinary framework. In the name of the restaurant, a plus sign instead of “and” or “or” is used. This sign symbolizes a collaborative and equal partnership between Myers and Chang. Myers brings front-of-house restaurant hospitality experience, while Chang brings expertise in culinary and baking arts. Their shared collaboration highlights their effort in combining different tastes by drawing inspiration from a broad spectrum of Chinese and Southeast Asian traditions.

"Ours is a simple endeavor. We are a neighborhood restaurant doing our own thing with great ingredients and a lovely gathering of people. “Asian-ish,” if you need a label." - From the official website of Myers + Chang

On its website, Myers + Chang writes, "Ours is a simple endeavor. We are a neighborhood restaurant doing our own thing with great ingredients and a lovely gathering of people. “Asian-ish,” if you need a label." Its self-description of “Asian-ish” is another deliberate language choice. It is an expression of how the restaurant playfully defies the traditional notions of authenticity in favor of a creative and cross-cultural cuisine. This self-positioning acts as a purposeful linguistic cue that the food is not confined by rigid national boundaries or recipes. The term also enables the couple to combine Taiwanese, Chinese, Thai, and Vietnamese flavor profiles and personal American comfort food traditions without feeling pressure to recreate fully authentic and traditional Asian dishes. What’s more, the informal ending -ish unites different cultural backgrounds in a unified narrative. By framing itself as an Asian-ish space, the restaurant becomes a hybrid environment where customers of diverse backgrounds are welcome. Overall, the restaurant’s name and self-positioning highlight its commitment to collaboration, inclusivity, and accessibility.

Culinary Terms, Cultural References, and Artistic Elements

Myers + Chang Food Menu Field Observation Photograph
Myers + Chang Beverages Menu Field Observation Photograph
Nasi Goreng (Indonesian Fried Rice) Field Observation Photograph

The menu of the restaurant deserves special attention as it is the main written text through which the restaurant constructs its “Asian-ish” identity. There are dishes labeled with regional and cultural specificity, such as wok-charred Cantonese Cauliflower, Hakka Eggplant, Shanghai hand-pulled noodles, Taiwanese Cool Dan Dan Noodles, Korean Fried Chicken Bun, and Vietnamese Iced Coffee. The menu explicitly shows that the couple does not confine themselves to a single, rigid regional culinary tradition. Instead, they serve customers “Asian-ish” cuisine that combines the unique flavor profiles of Taiwanese, Chinese, Southeast Asian, and Korean comfort foods.

The menu uses a specialized vocabulary, such as dan dan, nasi goreng, junmai genshu, nigori, and yuzu. Dan Dan is a spicy noodle dish originating from Sichuan, China. Nasi goerng is an Indonesian fried rice dish. junmai genshu and nigori are Japanese sake. Yuzu is an aromatic citrus originating from East Asia. Customers from the regions where the dishes or beverages originate are familiar with the terms. However, American customers need a certain level of literacy to navigate these dishes. Kevin, a server, told me, "This specialized vocabulary shows our effort to honor diverse culinary traditions and celebrate a fluid, multicultural identity."

At the same time, the restaurant keeps itself familiar to American customers. The menu uses a lot of abbreviations. V/V stands for vegetarian/vegan, GF represents gluten-free, NF means nut-free, and SF refers to shellfish-free. The application of abbreviations in the menu is a form of specialized literacy available only to diners who have prior knowledge of modern American food discourse. These abbreviations play practical and rhetorical roles in indicating inclusivity. Even American customers who are unfamiliar with cultural references in the menu can feel welcome at the restaurant because the use of these abbreviations celebrates a health-conscious, modern dining culture that is popular in contemporary America.

Front Window Dragon & Dining Tables Field Observation Photograph
Painted Tiger & Long Counter Field Observation Photograph
Framed Artwork on Restaurant Walls Field Observation Photograph

Myers + Chang develops its Asian-ish identity by adopting Asian arts as an aesthetic of playfulness and multi-layeredness instead of traditionalism. The visual language of the restaurant is characterized by bright, cartoonish murals of pink and orange dragons, which scroll all over its windows and give an instant Asian-inspired sense of sensibility to passing people. The interior has painted tigers and dragons. In my interview with Gabby, the manager of Myers and Chang, she explained that the restaurant intentionally uses Asian cultural images throughout the space. "Decorations like dragons and tigers are intended to contribute to the restaurant's identity rather than simply filling empty wall space," she told me.

The decoration of the restaurant does not simply end with the cartoonish dragon and tiger, but adds portraits of Asian and Japanese women to make the restaurant look even more Asian-ish through a familiar language of Asian visuals, just like how the menu draws on Chinese, Taiwanese, Thai, and Vietnamese traditions without being completely authentic.

The restaurant's decorative style blends classic Asian iconography with modern, playful graphics. Combining these traditional, figurative elements with new, playful graphics lets Myers + Chang create an environment that feels both familiar and novel, supporting the restaurant's identity as a creative, personal interpretation of Asian iconography rather than a direct portrayal of any single Asian culture.

The kitchen of Myers + Chang is partly open and visible from the dining area. I could see employees preparing food behind the long counter. A long counter with high chairs runs alongside the kitchen. This is a typical American diner layout. It designs its seating and menus in the format of family-style dining and uses big communal tables for customers to share plates, a practice that reflects Eastern traditions of collective dining and community gathering. Obviously, Myers + Chang is a transcultural space that perfectly bridges Asian and American cultural conventions.

Written Communication and Myers+Chang at Home

Cookbook Displayed on Restaurant Shelf Field Observation Photograph
Myers+Chang at Home By Joanne Chang

The restaurant’s written communication extends from its name and menu to its cookbook, Myers+Chang at Home: Recipes from the Beloved Boston Eatery. I saw this cookbook, written by its founder Chang, displayed on the shelf as soon as I entered the restaurant. Gabby said, "This cookbook aims to bring the recipes and the ethos of the restaurant to a format accessible to home cooks." Obviously, this process of textual production makes the temporality of the dining experience permanent at Myers+Chang in the form of durable literacy circulating outside the walls of the restaurant. What’s more, the cookbook makes the professional knowledge of the kitchen accessible to the home cooks. According to Gabby, both adventurous home cooks and longtime fans of the restaurant are the target audience of this cookbook. In this sense, the cookbook transforms the restaurant from a physical place into a written text, allowing anyone with English literacy to engage with the restaurant’s unique Asian-ish culture and cuisine.

I noticed that this restaurant highlighted its “Asian-ish” identity on various social media platforms. Gabby told me that I could order their food on Toast. On its Toast ordering page, it is written, “Ours is a simple endeavor. We are a neighborhood restaurant doing our own thing with great ingredients and a lovely gathering of people. “Asian-ish,” if you need a label.” By using the same label of Asian-ish across various social media platforms, the restaurant successfully makes “Asian-ish” its textual signature and a recognized brand marker.

Oral Communication at Myers + Chang

Myers + Chang Bar & Open Counter Field Observation Photograph
Counter Seating & Staff Interaction Field Observation Photograph

Not only the written texts but also the oral communication that happens at Myers + Chang show the couple’s celebration of multiculturalism. During my visit to Myers and Chang, I communicated with several waiters and waitresses. Most of them are fluent not only in English but also in another language. Some staff speak fluent Mandarin; one speaks Cantonese, and one speaks Vietnamese. There are also a Japanese and a Korean waitress. The staff’s fluency in different languages is a sign that multilingualism is not just working on the menu of the restaurant but on its floor as well. It also shows the restaurant’s insistence on its Asian-ish identity.

For customers from Asian backgrounds, they can always find a waiter or waitress who speaks the same language as they do at Myers + Chang. Kevin told me, "We want customers to feel welcomed and comfortable, similar to being in a family or parent's kitchen. Knowing their language helps." Gabby, the manager, said to me, "Our goal is to create a friendly, passionate Asian-diner experience where customers feel comfortable asking questions. We know many customers want their questions to be answered in their mother tongues." I met two Chinese customers who spoke "Broken English" like Amy Tan's mother. They told me that they feel at ease at Myers + Chang because waiters who speak Chinese here can easily understand them. As Zadie Smith writes in her writing, her original childhood voice faded away as she learned to speak a polished and formal English accent at Cambridge University. The two Chinese customers said to me, "We proudly speak in our mother tongue at Myers + Chang. The waiters talk to us in Mandarin." This further lets me realize that employing culturally diverse staff is a concrete step the restaurant takes toward inclusivity.

Ending Words

Myers + Chang rely on language and literacy to create a hybrid identity that is both embedded in the Asian culinary culture and expressed in the American cultural context. The naming, self-description, menu, staff communication, and cookbook all constitute a literate ecosystem in which bilingualism, culinary terms, cultural references, and artistic elements form a particular form of dining literacy: a type of literacy that asks customers to read across languages, interpret cultural references, learn about Asian art genres, and embrace hybridity. This literacy is not incidental but part of the dining experience.

The restaurant combines Asian and American rhetorical strategies in its linguistic and artistic practice just as the cuisine combines Asian and American. That way, Myers + Chang is as Asian-ish in its literate practices, including naming, menu design, restaurant decoration, and narratives, as it is in its food, forming a harmonious ecosystem where language, culture, arts, and taste are mutually enriching of each other.
